title: Circle Theorems
concept: Six circle facts cover every SAT circle problem. Arc length = (θ/360) × 2πr — the fraction of the circumference. Sector area = (θ/360) × πr² — the same fraction applied to the full area. Central angle theorem: a central angle equals, in degrees, the arc it intercepts. Inscribed angle theorem: an inscribed angle is exactly half the central angle that intercepts the same arc — the vertex is on the circle, not at the center. Circle equation: (x−h)²+(y−k)²=r², where (h,k) is the center; when the equation is expanded, complete the square to recover h, k, and r. Tangent–radius: a tangent to a circle is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact, giving a right angle you can use with the Pythagorean theorem. For all arc and sector problems on the SAT, use π≈3.14 and choose dimensions that produce clean decimal answers.

workedExamples.problem: A circular track has radius 10 meters. A runner jogs along an arc that subtends a central angle of 90°. Using π≈3.14, what is the length of the arc?
The equation of a circle is x²+y²+10x−6y+9=0. What is the radius of the circle?
steps: Complete the square: add (10/2)²=25 for x and (−6/2)²=9 for y to both sides.

trapPatterns: used_diameter_not_radius: plugging the diameter into a formula that requires the radius — arc and sector formulas both use r, not 2r.
arc_vs_sector: computing arc length when sector area is asked (or vice versa) — both use (θ/360) but arc multiplies by 2πr while sector multiplies by πr².
central_vs_inscribed: using the full arc measure as the inscribed angle — the inscribed angle is always half the central angle for the same arc.
forgot_to_complete_square: reading h, k, and r directly from the expanded equation x²+y²+bx+cy+d=0 without completing the square.
sign_error_on_center: from (x+4)²+(y−3)²=49, reading the center as (4,3) instead of (−4,3) — the center coordinate negates the sign in the bracket.
calculatorStrategy: use_desmos_graph for arc and sector problems — type the formula directly (e.g., (90/360)*2*3.14*10) for instant results. solve_algebraically for circle equations, central/inscribed angle, and tangent problems — these reduce to one or two arithmetic steps with no calculator needed.

problems.question: A circular running track has a radius of 10 meters. A runner jogs along an arc that subtends a central angle of 90° at the center. Using π≈3.14, what is the length of the arc, in meters?

choices.label: B
choices.trap: used_diameter_not_radius: used diameter (20) instead of radius (10) — (90/360)×2×3.14×20=31.4.

choices.label: C
choices.trap: arc_vs_sector: computed sector area instead of arc length — (90/360)×3.14×10²=78.5.

choices.label: D
choices.trap: forgot_fraction: computed the full circumference (2×3.14×10=62.8) without multiplying by θ/360.

explanation: Arc length = (θ/360) × 2πr.
Fraction of circle: 90/360 = 1/4.
Trap B (31.4): used diameter 20 instead of radius 10.
Trap C (78.5): used the sector area formula πr² instead of arc length 2πr.
Trap D (62.8): forgot the 90/360 fraction — that is the full circumference.

problems.question: A Ferris wheel is divided into two arcs by two spokes that pass through the center. The major arc (the longer portion) measures 230°. What is the measure, in degrees, of the central angle that intercepts the minor arc?
explanation: The two arcs of a circle must sum to 360°.
The central angle theorem: a central angle equals the arc it intercepts.
So the central angle is also 130°.
Trap: 180−230 is negative — that applies to supplementary angles, not arcs of a circle.

problems.question: A circular pizza has a radius of 10 inches and is cut into 10 equal slices. Using π≈3.14, what is the area of one slice, in square inches?

choices.label: B
choices.trap: arc_vs_sector: computed arc length instead of sector area — (36/360)×2×3.14×10=6.28.

choices.label: C
choices.trap: forgot_fraction: computed the full pizza area (3.14×10²=314) without dividing by 10 slices.

choices.label: D
choices.trap: used_diameter_not_radius: used diameter (20) in the area formula — (36/360)×3.14×20²=125.6.

explanation: 10 equal slices → each slice is 360°/10 = 36° of the circle.
Trap B (6.28): arc length formula uses 2πr, not πr² — gives the curved edge, not the area.
Trap C (314): the full pizza area; forgot to take 1/10 of it.
Trap D (125.6): used diameter 20 instead of radius 10 in r².

problems.calculatorStrategy: use_desmos_graph — type (36/360)*2*3.14*50 into Desmos for the multiplication.
problems.question: A runner on a circular track with radius 50 meters jogs along an arc that subtends a central angle of 36° at the center. Using π≈3.14, what is the length of the arc, in meters?
explanation: Arc length = (θ/360) × 2πr.
Fraction of circle: 36/360 = 1/10.
Trap: using the sector area formula gives (1/10)×3.14×2500=785 — completely different magnitude.
Trap: forgetting the θ/360 factor gives the full circumference 2×3.14×50=314.

problems.calculatorStrategy: solve_algebraically — halve the central angle, one step.
problems.question: On a Ferris wheel modeled as a circle, the central angle AOB measures 80°. A rider sits at point C on the rim of the wheel (on the major arc), looking toward the arc AB. What is the measure of inscribed angle ACB?

choices.label: B
choices.trap: central_vs_inscribed: used the central angle measure directly — inscribed angle is always half the central angle for the same arc.

choices.label: C
choices.trap: doubled_central: multiplied the central angle by 2 instead of halving — reversed the inscribed angle theorem.

choices.label: D
choices.trap: halved_twice: applied the halving rule twice (80÷2÷2=20), treating inscribed as 1/4 of the central angle.

explanation: Inscribed angle theorem: an inscribed angle is half the central angle intercepting the same arc.
Central angle AOB = 80°.
Inscribed angle ACB = 80° ÷ 2 = 40°.
Trap B (80): using the central angle value directly — the inscribed angle is not equal to the central angle.
Trap C (160): doubled instead of halved — that would give the reflex central angle.
Trap D (20): applied halving twice; the theorem halves once only.

problems.calculatorStrategy: solve_algebraically — read directly from standard form; watch for sign flip on center coordinates.
problems.question: A cell tower's circular coverage area is modeled by the equation (x+4)²+(y−3)²=49. What is the x-coordinate of the center of this circle?

choices.label: B
choices.trap: sign_error_on_center: read the center as +4 from (x+4)² — the standard form is (x−h)², so (x+4)²=(x−(−4))² means h=−4.

choices.label: C
choices.trap: used_radius: reported the radius (√49=7) instead of the x-coordinate of the center.

choices.label: D
choices.trap: used_r_squared: reported r²=49 directly instead of computing the center coordinate.

explanation: Standard form: (x−h)²+(y−k)²=r², where (h,k) is the center.
The x-coordinate of the center is −4.
Trap B (+4): the +4 inside the bracket becomes −4 for the center — the sign flips.
Trap C (7): √49=7 is the radius, not the center coordinate.
Trap D (49): 49 is r², not the center.

problems.calculatorStrategy: solve_algebraically — complete the square on both x and y terms, then take the square root.
problems.question: The equation of a circle is x²+y²+10x−6y+9=0. What is the radius of the circle?
explanation: Rearrange: (x²+10x) + (y²−6y) = −9.
Complete the square — add (10/2)²=25 to both sides for x, and (−6/2)²=9 for y:
r²=25, so r=5.
Trap r=3: reading the constant 9 directly as r² (forgot_to_complete_square — the completion adds 25+9=34, changing the right side from 9 to 25).
Trap r=25: forgot to take the square root; reported r²=25 as the radius.

problems.calculatorStrategy: solve_algebraically — apply the tangent-radius theorem to identify the right angle, then use the Pythagorean theorem.
problems.question: A cable is stretched from an external point P to touch a circular reel at point T. The center of the reel is O, and the radius OT is 8 feet. The distance OP is 17 feet. What is the length, in feet, of the cable PT?

choices.label: B
choices.trap: no_pythagorean: computed PT=OP−OT=17−8=9, subtracting lengths linearly instead of using the Pythagorean theorem.

choices.label: C
choices.trap: added_instead: computed PT=OP+OT=17+8=25, adding the two lengths instead of applying the theorem.

choices.label: D
choices.trap: wrong_pythagorean: computed √(OP²+OT²)=√(289+64)=√353≈19, adding the squares instead of subtracting (used the wrong leg as hypotenuse).

explanation: Tangent–radius theorem: a tangent line is perpendicular to the radius at the point of tangency.
PT⊥OT, so triangle OTP is a right triangle with the right angle at T.
OP is the hypotenuse (the side opposite the right angle): OP=17, OT=8.
PT² = OP²−OT² = 289−64 = 225 → PT = 15 feet.
This is the 8-15-17 Pythagorean triple: 8²+15²=64+225=289=17². ✓
Trap B (9): subtracted lengths directly — Pythagorean theorem subtracts squares, not lengths.
Trap C (25): added the lengths, which gives neither a leg nor the hypotenuse.
Trap D (19): added the squares (OP²+OT²) instead of subtracting — treats OT as a second leg when OT is one leg and OP is the hypotenuse.
